title: Credential split across adjacent or added string literals
summary: A SendGrid-shaped key is written as two string pieces that the language joins: adjacent literals in Python, or two literals added with the plus operator in JavaScript and Python.
rationale: The language concatenates the pieces, so the program holds the intact key although no single literal in the file does. The pieces are separated by closing and opening quotes, whitespace or an operator, which are outside the fragments. This is explicit concatenation, a different mechanism from a line continuation inside one literal.

expectation.rationale: Flagged, with every fragment covered. The Python reference (adjacent literals have the meaning of their concatenation; the plus operator concatenates at run time) and the ECMAScript specification (the plus operator returns the string-concatenation of two strings) are both consistent with the reading. Stated as consistency of two texts, not as a provider rule. Concatenation with a non-literal operand (a variable, a call) is not covered: the fixtures use literals only. Synthetic, never issued: every value in the fixtures is built from the words SYNTHETIC and EXAMPLE, so none can authenticate.

sources.supports: Multiple adjacent string literals have the meaning of their concatenation; to concatenate string expressions at run time the plus operator may be used.
The addition operator returns the string-concatenation of its operands when either primitive operand is a String.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed.
